rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Your Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) before the birth covers the last six weeks before the delivery. The law says the employer may not employ a pregnant woman "in den letzten sechs Wochen vor der Entbindung" (in the last six weeks before delivery). This is called the "Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung".

The period is counted from the expected date of delivery shown in a certificate from a doctor, midwife or male midwife ("der voraussichtliche Tag der Entbindung … wie er sich aus dem ärztlichen Zeugnis oder dem Zeugnis einer Hebamme oder eines Entbindungspflegers ergibt"). With an expected date of 15 November 2026, six weeks earlier falls at the start of October 2026. The excerpts do not say exactly how the first day is counted, so check the exact start date against your certificate.

Three further points from the same section:

- You may keep working during these six weeks only if you expressly declare that you are willing to. You can withdraw that declaration at any time, with effect for the future.
- If the baby is not born on the expected date, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match.
- After the birth, the employer may not employ you until eight weeks have passed. This extends to twelve weeks in three cases: a premature birth, a multiple birth, or a disability in the child within the meaning of § 2(1) sentence 1 SGB IX that a doctor confirms before eight weeks after the birth. The disability extension applies only if you apply for it. If the baby arrives early, the period after the birth is also extended by the time lost before the birth.

Your employer must not employ you during this period. Maternity pay for this period is paid by your health insurance fund (Krankenkasse). The certificate stating the expected delivery date is what counts for payment before the birth.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) must be applied for in writing. It is paid backdated only for the last three months of the child's life before the month of life in which your application is received. Months of life further back than that are not paid. The law does not set a fixed cut-off for applying; the consequence is that any earlier months are lost.

The months counted here are the child's months of life, not calendar months. Elterngeld can be received from the day of birth.

Whether and how much you receive in your case is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for your area.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, how much notice you give for Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) depends on when the leave falls. You must request it from your employer in text form at the latest:

- 7 weeks before it starts, for leave up to the child's third birthday ("spätestens sieben Wochen").
- 13 weeks before it starts, for leave between the child's third birthday and the end of their eighth year ("spätestens 13 Wochen").

When you request leave falling before the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take as Elternzeit.

Where there are urgent reasons, a reasonable shorter period is possible by exception ("Bei dringenden Gründen ist ausnahmsweise eine angemessene kürzere Frist möglich"). The law does not set a fixed length for this shorter period.

The official family portal explains that "text form" means a letter without a signature or an email is also enough. That page also describes a different notice rule for children born before 1 July 2015. The statute excerpts here do not include the provision behind that, so it is not covered here.

Your employer must confirm your Elternzeit to you ("Der Arbeitgeber hat ... die Elternzeit zu bescheinigen").

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, the period after the birth in which an employer may not employ a woman is normally eight weeks: "bis zum Ablauf von acht Wochen nach der Entbindung" (MuSchG §3(2)). An early birth affects this in two ways.

First, the eight weeks become twelve weeks in each of three cases: "bei Frühgeburten" (premature births), "bei Mehrlingsgeburten" (multiple births), and where a disability in the child is medically established before the eight weeks end. In the disability case, the statute says the extension applies only if the woman applies for it ("nur, wenn die Frau dies beantragt").

Second, if the baby arrives before the expected date, the six-week period before the birth is shortened accordingly. The period after the birth, whether eight or twelve weeks, is then extended by the time that was lost before the birth: "verlängert sich die Schutzfrist nach der Entbindung ... um den Zeitraum der Verkürzung der Schutzfrist vor der Entbindung" (MuSchG §3(1) and (2)).

The Familienportal explains the difference in plain terms. A baby born somewhat before the expected date, but not medically premature, still gives a total Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) of 14 weeks, with the days missed before the birth added after it. A baby that counts medically as premature, for example one weighing less than 2,500 grams at birth, gives 12 weeks after the birth, raising the total from 14 to 18 weeks. The statute itself does not define a premature birth; the 2,500-gram figure is the portal's example.

After the birth, the ban on work cannot be waived, except for pupils and students who expressly ask to resume their training. If an employer asks you to work during Mutterschutz, the Familienportal says you can contact your Aufsichtsbehörde (supervisory authority).

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. Under federal law, Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) means a dismissal by your employer is not permitted ("Die Kündigung gegenüber einer Frau ist unzulässig") in three periods:

1. during pregnancy;
2. until four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy;
3. until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth.

This protection applies only if your employer knew about the pregnancy, miscarriage or birth when dismissing you, or if you tell them within two weeks of receiving the dismissal ("innerhalb von zwei Wochen nach Zugang der Kündigung"). Missing the two weeks does no harm if it was not your fault and you inform them without delay. The same rules apply to steps an employer takes to prepare a dismissal. The official guidance adds that you must already have been pregnant when you received the dismissal, but you are protected even if you did not yet know.

There is one exception. In special cases not connected with the woman's condition during pregnancy, after a miscarriage or after the birth, the supreme state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can exceptionally declare a dismissal admissible ("ausnahmsweise die Kündigung für zulässig erklären"). The dismissal must then be in writing and state the reason. The official guidance gives examples such as insolvency, partial closure of the business, a small business that cannot continue without a qualified replacement, or a particularly serious breach of duty. Without the supervisory authority's consent, the dismissal is invalid ("Ohne die Zustimmung der Aufsichtsbehörde ist die Kündigung unwirksam").

If you are dismissed without that consent, the guidance says you must bring a claim before the competent labour court, "normalerweise innerhalb von 3 Wochen" (normally within 3 weeks) of receiving the written dismissal. If you do not bring a claim, the dismissal is treated as valid. You can bring the claim yourself or through a lawyer, in writing or orally at the court office. The guidance also says you should involve the competent supervisory authority. If the authority consented to the dismissal, you can challenge that consent separately, depending on the state by objection or by court action. This does not replace the labour court claim.

If you take parental leave after the birth, protection against dismissal can be extended.

Whether a dismissal in your own situation is permitted is not something this answer can decide. That lies with the supervisory authority for maternity protection in your state and, if challenged, the labour court.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. The law sets an income limit above which the claim to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses.

The rule in the statute. A claim lapses if the entitled person had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of more than 175,000 euros in the last completed tax assessment period before the child's birth ("ein zu versteuerndes Einkommen ... in Höhe von mehr als 175 000 Euro", BEEG §1(8)). If another person also meets the conditions, for example the other parent living in the same household, the limit applies to the combined figure. The claim lapses if "die Summe des zu versteuernden Einkommens beider Personen mehr als 175 000 Euro beträgt" (BEEG §1(8)).

Taxable income is not gross pay. The federal guidance page explains that zu versteuerndes Einkommen is usually well below gross income. It is calculated after deductions such as special expenses, pension and insurance contributions, individual allowances and extraordinary burdens. The tax office (Finanzamt) determines it, and it appears on your tax assessment notice. The same page says that notice for the calendar year before the birth should be attached to the Elterngeld application where one exists.

If the tax assessment notice is not yet available. The statute provides that if it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the amount of Elterngeld is decided provisionally until proof is supplied (BEEG §8(3)). Where the application states the limit is likely not exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if the limit turns out to be exceeded (BEEG §8(2)).

Earlier births. The federal guidance page describes different, higher limits for births before the current rule. The statute's transitional provision for earlier births is not among the sources I was given, so I cannot say which limit applies to a particular birth date.

Which limit applies to your child's birth, and whether your household is above or below it, is decided by the Elterngeldstelle (parental allowance office) for your district.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
The number of months is set by federal law, BEEG §4. It depends on which form of Elterngeld (parental allowance) is taken and how the months are split between the parents.

Basic months. Parents together are entitled to twelve monthly payments of basic Elterngeld ("Die Eltern haben gemeinsam Anspruch auf zwölf Monatsbeträge Basiselterngeld"). They are jointly entitled to two further months if one parent's earned income is reduced in two months of the child's life ("zwei weitere Monate Basiselterngeld (Partnermonate)"). That makes 14 basic months in total.

Swapping for the longer, lower variant. Instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus ("jeweils zwei Lebensmonate Elterngeld Plus").

Limits per parent. One parent can receive at most twelve monthly payments of basic Elterngeld, plus at most four monthly payments of the partnership bonus under BEEG §4b ("höchstens vier zustehenden Monatsbeträge Partnerschaftsbonus nach § 4b"). The conditions for that bonus are set in §4b, which is not among the excerpts. The federal family portal describes it as up to 4 extra months of Elterngeld Plus for each parent when both work part-time at the same time. A parent is only entitled to Elterngeld if they take it for at least two months of the child's life.

Months that count as used. Months in which a parent receives certain benefits that are offset against Elterngeld, such as maternity benefits, count as months of basic Elterngeld (BEEG §4(4)).

Time windows. Basic Elterngeld can be received until the child completes its 14th month of life. Elterngeld Plus can be received until the 32nd month, as long as at least one parent takes it in consecutive months from the 15th month ("in aufeinander folgenden Lebensmonaten").

Premature births. For a child born well before the expected date of delivery, the joint basic entitlement is higher:
- at least 6 weeks early: 13 months
- at least 8 weeks early: 14 months
- at least 12 weeks early: 15 months
- at least 16 weeks early: 16 months
The per-parent maximum and the time windows extend to match. The expected date is the one shown in the doctor's or midwife's certificate.

These are the rules the law sets for everyone. How many months your family receives depends on your circumstances and on what you apply for. That is decided by the Elterngeldstelle for your district, not here.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) gives each parent extra months of payment when both work part-time at the same time. The law describes it as "einen zusätzlichen Monatsbetrag Elterngeld Plus": an additional monthly amount of the plus variant of parental allowance, per parent, per month of the child's life.

Who qualifies, under BEEG §4b. Both parents must meet both of these conditions:
1. Each works "nicht weniger als 24 und nicht mehr als 32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats", that is, at least 24 and at most 32 hours a week, averaged over the child's month of life.
2. Each meets the general conditions of BEEG §1. Those conditions are not in the excerpts I have.

How it can be taken:
- Each parent can receive at most four bonus months.
- It can only be received if it is taken for at least two months.
- The parents can only take it at the same time and in consecutive months of the child's life.
- The consecutive-months requirement counts as met even if it later turns out that the conditions were not met in every month for which the bonus was applied.

The official guidance page explains the averaging: you do not need to work 24 to 32 hours in every single week. What counts is the average over the month. It also says that if one parent works under 24 or over 32 hours in a month, both parents lose the bonus for that month. Payment for the other months is kept, provided the conditions are met in at least two months.

A single parent (BEEG §4c). A parent can take the bonus alone in any one of these three situations:
1. The parent meets the conditions for the single-parent tax relief under §24b(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act, and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child.
2. Care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare within the meaning of §1666(1) and (2) of the Civil Code.
3. Care by the other parent is impossible, in particular because of serious illness or severe disability. Economic reasons and being busy with other activities do not count.

In that case, a parent who works 24 to 32 hours a week on average in at least two and at most four consecutive months receives the additional monthly amounts for those months. If one of these situations arises while both parents are already receiving the bonus, one parent can continue it alone.

Amount. The guidance page says the bonus is calculated like the plus variant, and comes to between 150 and 900 euros a month per parent, depending on income before the birth.

The guidance also says that for children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply. Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided only by the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your district.

rows.question: We forgot to apply for Kindergeld. How far back will they pay?
rows.reply:
Kindergeld (child benefit) is paid backdated for at most six months. The law says payment is made retroactively "nur für die letzten sechs Monate vor Beginn des Monats, in dem der Antrag auf Kindergeld eingegangen ist": only for the last six months before the start of the month in which the application is received. The same provision states that the entitlement to Kindergeld itself is not affected by this payment limit ("bleibt von dieser Auszahlungsbeschränkung unberührt"). The limit applies to what is paid out, not to whether the entitlement existed.

The source does not set an application deadline. What it describes is a consequence: the later the application arrives, the more of the earlier months fall outside the six-month window.

Kindergeld must be applied for in writing at the responsible Familienkasse. The official family portal says to submit it to the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit. For a backdated claim, it says to state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when you want to receive Kindergeld.

Whether you were entitled for a given month, and which months are paid, is decided by the Familienkasse, not by this service.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The law sets a one-week period. Under PStG §18(1), the birth of a child must be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born "binnen einer Woche" (within one week).

The report can be made in one of two ways:
- by the persons named in PStG §19, orally or in writing, or
- by the institutions named in PStG §20, in writing.

Where a person makes the report, they must substantiate the birth ("die Geburt des Kindes glaubhaft zu machen"). The excerpts do not name the persons in §19 or the institutions in §20.

The official family portal adds that if your child is born in a hospital, birth centre or maternity clinic, the facility notifies the responsible Standesamt and sends the birth certificate issued at the birth. If your child is born at home, the midwife or doctor issues that certificate, and you must present it to the Standesamt within one week.

One of the portal's checklists describes the period as "7 Werktagen" (7 working days). The statute says "binnen einer Woche" (within one week), and the statute governs.

For a stillborn child, PStG §18(1) requires the report "spätestens am dritten auf die Geburt folgenden Werktag" (at the latest on the third working day after the birth).

rows.reply:

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Under statutory health insurance law, an insured woman is entitled to midwife assistance. SGB V §24d says she has a claim during pregnancy, at the birth and after the birth to medical care and to midwife assistance ("Anspruch auf ärztliche Betreuung sowie auf Hebammenhilfe"). If the mother cannot look after the child after the birth, the insured child has its own claim to the midwife services that relate to the child.

The Familienportal puts it this way: every woman with statutory health insurance is entitled to support from a Hebamme (midwife). If you are privately insured, the same page says to check with your insurer beforehand which services it covers. Private insurance is outside what this product covers.

Whether you have this entitlement in your own case is decided by your Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer). Ask your Krankenkasse directly about your own cover.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The first check-ups are set out in the Kinder-Richtlinie (children's screening directive) of the Gemeinsamer Bundesausschuss (G-BA). It provides for ten examinations in the first six years of life, called U1 to U9 (including U7a). Each Vorsorgeuntersuchung (routine preventive check-up) has a set period and a tolerance limit around it.

The first ones are:

- U1: immediately after the birth ("Unmittelbar nach der Geburt"). It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the baby is born ("innerhalb der ersten 30 Minuten nach der Geburt"). If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should do it.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life (tolerance limit: 3rd to 14th day).
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life (tolerance limit: 3rd to 8th week).
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life (tolerance limit: 2nd to 4½ months).
- U5: 6th to 7th month of life (tolerance limit: 5th to 8th month).
- U6: 10th to 12th month of life (tolerance limit: 9th to 14th month).

The directive says the examinations can only be taken up within these periods, taking the tolerance limits into account ("können nur in den jeweils angegebenen Zeiträumen unter Berücksichtigung folgender Toleranzgrenzen in Anspruch genommen werden").

If your baby is born early, the same periods apply ("Auch bei Frühgeborenen sind die Untersuchungszeiträume einzuhalten"). Being born early is taken into account when the results are assessed.

The directive also says the examinations may only be carried out by doctors who have the knowledge, experience, professional authorisation and equipment to provide them.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the maternity protection periods before and after the birth, plus the day of birth itself.

Who pays it depends on how you are insured:

- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, you receive Mutterschaftsgeld under the rules of the Social Code Book V (MuSchG §19(1)). Under those rules it is paid "für die Zeit der Schutzfrist nach § 3 des Mutterschutzgesetzes sowie für den Entbindungstag" (SGB V §24i(3)). For women employed when the protection period before the birth begins, it is based on average net daily pay over the last three settled calendar months, and is "höchstens 13 Euro für den Kalendertag" (SGB V §24i(2)).
- If your average net daily pay is above 13 euros, the employer pays the difference as a Zuschuss zum Mutterschaftsgeld (MuSchG §20(1); SGB V §24i(2)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, Mutterschaftsgeld is paid by the federal government, but "insgesamt höchstens 210 Euro". It is paid "auf Antrag vom Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung", so in this case it is paid on application to the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung (MuSchG §19(2)).

On timing, the official family portal says the protection periods "beginnen normalerweise 6 Wochen vor dem errechneten Geburtstermin und enden 8 Wochen nach der Geburt". For payment before the birth, the decisive document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife stating the expected date of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)).

The excerpts do not say when or how to apply to a statutory health insurer, and they set no application deadline. For that, ask your own statutory health insurer. If you are not statutorily insured, the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung is the body that pays on application. Whether you qualify, and how much you would receive, is decided by the paying body, not here.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No, not automatically. Under BGB §1592, the father of a child is the man who: 1. is married to the mother at the time of the birth ("zum Zeitpunkt der Geburt mit der Mutter des Kindes verheiratet ist"); 2. has acknowledged paternity ("die Vaterschaft anerkannt hat"); or 3. has had his paternity established by a court ("gerichtlich festgestellt").

If you are not married at the birth, the first ground does not apply. Your partner becomes the legal father either through a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) or through a court decision. The federal family portal states that the acknowledgement requires the mother's consent.

Under BGB §1594:
- The acknowledgement can be made before the child is born ("schon vor der Geburt des Kindes zulässig").
- An acknowledgement made subject to a condition or a time limit is invalid.
- It is not effective while another man's paternity exists.
- Its legal effects can only be relied on from the time it becomes effective.

The father must make the declaration in person at a competent office. Examples are the local youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. Depending on the federal state, acknowledgement at a notary or local court may cost a fee.

Acknowledging paternity does not automatically give the father parental custody. The family portal says this also requires declarations by both parents that they want joint custody, or a court decision. Your local youth welfare office advises on custody questions.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody from birth. The law gives three ways for unmarried parents to get joint custody (BGB §1626a(1)):

1. Both parents declare that they want to take on custody jointly. These are called Sorgeerklärungen (declaration of joint custody). The statute says: "wenn sie erklären, dass sie die Sorge gemeinsam übernehmen wollen (Sorgeerklärungen)".
2. The parents marry each other.
3. The family court transfers custody to both parents jointly.

Otherwise, the mother keeps sole custody (BGB §1626a(3)).

The other parent must first be legally recognised as the father. This happens either when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Recognising paternity does not by itself give custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

On the court route, one parent applies. The family court transfers joint custody, in whole or in part, if this does not contradict the child's welfare. If the other parent gives no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not contradict the child's welfare (BGB §1626a(2)). The family portal adds that the court then decides in a simplified procedure. In that procedure, the youth welfare office is not consulted and the parents are not heard in person.

Sorgeerklärungen and court decisions transferring joint custody are entered in a custody register kept by the youth welfare office (SGB VIII §58(1)).

The excerpts do not say where or in what form the Sorgeerklärung is made. Unmarried parents have a legal right to advice on making a Sorgeerklärung and on the court route (SGB VIII §18(2)). Your local youth welfare office is the authority to approach for this. Applications to transfer custody go to the family court.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Not simply because the baby is born here. German law gives two routes to German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) at birth, and each has conditions.

By descent: a child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit at birth if a parent holds German Staatsangehörigkeit (StAG §4(1)).

By birth in Germany to foreign parents: a child born in Germany to foreign parents acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit if one parent meets both of these conditions (StAG §4(3)):
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years ("seit fünf Jahren rechtmäßig seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt im Inland"), and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence ("ein unbefristetes Aufenthaltsrecht"), or, as a Swiss national or a family member of one, a residence permit under the 1999 EU–Switzerland free movement agreement.

If the conditions are met, the acquisition is entered in the birth register where the birth is recorded (StAG §4(3)).

How it is checked: when the birth is registered, the registry office asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence (PStV §34(1)). If the information given points that way, the registry office obtains written confirmation from the foreigners' authority that the information is correct and that the parent had five years of lawful habitual residence at the time of the birth (PStV §34(2)). It also obtains this confirmation if the parents give no information or the office doubts it. The registry office then examines whether the child acquired German Staatsangehörigkeit and records the result (PStV §34(3)).

If the child does not become German, residence rules apply instead. A residence permit can be granted to the child ex officio if one parent holds a residence permit, a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit. It is granted ex officio if, at the time of birth, both parents (or the parent with sole custody) hold one of these. If a parent is in Germany on a visa or visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends (AufenthG §33).

Whether your child meets these conditions is decided by the registry office that registers the birth, with information from your local foreigners' authority. These excerpts do not cover Indian citizenship for your child. For that, contact the Indian embassy or consulate responsible for where you live.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
The law sets out several rules for a child born in Germany to foreign parents. Which one applies to your child depends on your own residence status, and only the authorities decide that.

Residence permit rules for a child born in Germany (AufenthG §33):
- If one parent holds an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit), a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit, the child may be granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis on the authority's own initiative.
- If, at the time of birth, both parents (or the parent with sole custody) hold one of those permits, the child is granted the Aufenthaltserlaubnis on the authority's own initiative.
- If the mother or father holds a visa at the time of birth, or may stay without a visa, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or that lawful visa-free stay ends.

German citizenship by birth (StAG §4(3)):
A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires German citizenship by birth if one parent meets both of these conditions:
1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years, and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence, or holds a residence permit as a Swiss national (or a family member of one) under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement.
This acquisition is entered in the birth register.

When the birth is registered, the registry office asks whether a parent holds an unlimited right of residence or the Swiss free-movement permit. It then obtains written information from the immigration authority and checks whether the child acquired German citizenship (PStV §34).

Whether your child acquired German citizenship is checked by the registry office that registers the birth. Questions about your child's residence permit are for your local immigration authority (Ausländerbehörde). This answer does not assess your family's situation.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under federal law, Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is set off against Elterngeld (parental allowance). The law calls this crediting: "werden folgende Einnahmen angerechnet".

What is credited (BEEG §3(1) no. 1):
- Mutterschaftsgeld from statutory health insurance.
- The employer's supplement to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20.
- Both count only for the period "ab dem Tag der Geburt des Kindes", meaning from the day the child is born.

One exception: the one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros under MuSchG §19(2) is not credited. That is the payment the Federal Office for Social Security makes to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer.

How the crediting works:
- The general 300-euro amount that is otherwise protected from crediting does not apply to maternity benefits (BEEG §3(2): "soweit nicht Einnahmen nach Absatz 1 Satz 1 Nummer 1 bis 3 auf das Elterngeld anzurechnen sind").
- If maternity benefits cover only part of a month of the child's life, they are credited only against the matching part of that month's Elterngeld.
- The official family portal explains the result. Where Mutterschaftsgeld for the same child is higher than Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. Where Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld.
- The portal also says that months in which the mother receives maternity benefits for the same child count as months of the basic form of parental allowance. This applies even if the benefits are due for only one day of that month.
- The other parent is affected differently. According to the portal, the mother's maternity benefits are credited only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the other parent's.

How much this changes your own payment is decided by the Elterngeldstelle (parental allowance office) responsible for your district, not here.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, the law allows work while receiving Elterngeld (parental allowance), within limits.

Who qualifies: one condition for Elterngeld is that the person does "keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit" (no work, or no full-time work) (BEEG §1(1) no. 4).

What counts as not working full-time: the law names three grounds (BEEG §1(6)). A person is not in full-time work if any one of these applies:
1. their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week, averaged over the child's month of life ("32 Wochenstunden im Durchschnitt des Lebensmonats");
2. they are in employment for vocational training ("Beschäftigung zur Berufsbildung");
3. they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§ 23 and 43 of Book VIII of the Social Code ("Kindertagespflegeperson").

How income affects the amount: for months after the birth in which the person earns less on average than before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as the relevant percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this purpose, pre-birth income counts up to at most 2,770 euros (BEEG §2(3)).

The longer, lower-rate option: instead of one month of basic Elterngeld, a person can take two months of Elterngeld Plus (BEEG §4(3)). The official family portal notes this option can be worth considering for people working part-time (familienportal.de).

Reporting income: if the application states expected income from work during the payment period, the amount is decided provisionally (BEEG §8(3) no. 3). After the payment period ends, the actual income for that time must be proven (BEEG §8(1)). If the application says no income is expected and income is earned anyway, payment is made subject to revocation (BEEG §8(2)).

Older births: the family portal says its explanation covers children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, partly different rules apply, and it refers parents to their Elterngeld office (familienportal.de).

Whether you qualify and how much you would receive while working is decided by your Elterngeld office, not here.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where: The Bundeskindergeldgesetz says the application should be made at the Familienkasse responsible under § 13 ("bei der nach § 13 zuständigen Familienkasse"). § 13 makes the Familienkasse responsible for receiving the application and deciding the claim, and the relevant one is set by a fixed order:
- the Familienkasse in whose district the entitled person has their residence (Wohnsitz);
- if there is no residence in Germany, the one where they habitually stay;
- if neither, the one where they work;
- in all other cases, Familienkasse Bayern Nord.
The Familienportal puts this as applying at the Familienkasse of your Agentur für Arbeit.

How: The statute says Kindergeld (child benefit) is to be applied for in writing ("schriftlich zu beantragen"). The Familienportal adds these points:
- You can apply electronically or in writing, using the Familienkassen's form.
- You can fill the form in online, then print and sign it.
- For newborn children, you can apply fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand.
- The application must include your tax identification number (steuerliche Identifikationsnummer) and your child's.

The Bundesagentur für Arbeit says that for a child under 18, you normally only need to give these two tax ID numbers. For a child born abroad or living abroad, you should provide a copy of the foreign birth certificate, or another official document certifying the birth.

The Familienportal says Kindergeld can be paid retroactively for up to 6 months ("für bis zu 6 Monate rückwirkend"). If you want this, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when.

Who applies: Kindergeld is granted to only one person per child. If the child lives in the parents' common household, the parents decide between themselves who is the entitled person. If they make no decision, the family court decides on application. Besides the entitled person, anyone with a legitimate interest in the payment can also apply.

For questions about applying, the Familienportal gives the free service number of the Bundesagentur für Arbeit: 0800 4 555530. Whether Kindergeld is granted in your case is decided by the responsible Familienkasse.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply:
Bavaria is outside the states this product covers. We cover federal law, Hessen state procedures and the Indian consular track. For how Elterngeld (parental allowance) is applied for and handled in Bavaria, contact the Elterngeld office responsible for your district in Bavaria, or Bavaria's official state portal. Elterngeld itself is federal law, so the federal rules below apply in Bavaria too.

Who can claim. A person has a claim if they live or usually stay in Germany, live in one household with the child, care for and bring up the child themselves, and do no work or do not work full-time (BEEG §1(1)). A person is not working full-time if their working time does not exceed 32 hours a week on average over the child's month of life, if they are in vocational training, or if they work as a suitable childminder (BEEG §1(6)). People who are self-employed ("selbständig erwerbstätig") count as working even while they are temporarily not working (BEEG §1(6a)). The claim lapses if taxable income in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175,000 euros. Where another person also meets the conditions, the limit applies to both incomes combined (BEEG §1(8)).

How much. Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth. It is paid up to a maximum of 1,800 euros a month for full months of life in which the person has no income from work (BEEG §2(1)). Income from work counts positive income from two sources: employment, and agriculture and forestry, a trade or business, and self-employed work ("Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Gewerbebetrieb und selbständiger Arbeit"). It must be taxable in Germany (BEEG §2(1)). The percentage rises for income below 1,000 euros and falls, down to 65 percent, for income above 1,200 euros (BEEG §2(2)). The minimum is 300 euros (BEEG §2(4)).

How self-employed income is measured. The statute says this follows §§2c to 2f. The excerpts include only §2c, which covers employment income, and not the provision on self-employed income. They do not cover how self-employed income is assessed.

Provisional decisions and proof. The amount is decided provisionally in three cases (BEEG §8(3)):
1. The tax assessment for the last completed assessment period before the birth is not yet available, and it cannot yet be said whether the 175,000 euro limit is exceeded.
2. Income from work before the birth cannot be determined.
3. The person expects to have income from work during the payment period.

If the application gave expected income, actual income for that period must be proven after the payment period ends (BEEG §8(1)). Payment is made subject to revocation ("unter dem Vorbehalt des Widerrufs") in two cases. The first is where the person said they would have no income from work but then does. The second is where the tax assessment was missing and the 175,000 euro limit turns out to be exceeded (BEEG §8(2)).

Whether you are entitled, and how much you would receive, is decided only by the Elterngeld office responsible for your district in Bavaria.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
I cannot fill in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application. Completing it means choosing months and stating facts about your family, and only the responsible authority decides your individual case. What the law says the application involves:

- Elterngeld must be applied for in writing ("Elterngeld ist schriftlich zu beantragen", BEEG §7(1)).
- The application must state which months you claim as Basiselterngeld, which as Elterngeld Plus, and which as Partnerschaftsbonus (BEEG §7(1)).
- The person applying signs it. The other entitled parent also signs to confirm they are aware of it ("zur Bestätigung der Kenntnisnahme"). This does not apply in the case of §4c or where one parent alone has custody (BEEG §7(3)).
- The choices made in the application can be changed until the end of the payment period (BEEG §7(2)).
- Payment is made retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid (BEEG §7(1)).
- If you give expected earnings from work in the application, you must prove your actual earnings for that period once the payment period ends (BEEG §8(1)).
- The official family portal lists your child's birth certificate and proof of your previous income among the documents to include (familienportal.de).

The responsible authority is the one your Land has designated for the district where your child lives when you first apply (BEEG §12(1)). In practice this is the Elterngeldstelle for your district.

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
Whether your application will be approved is a decision about your individual case. Only the responsible authority can make it, so this answer gives the general rules, not a verdict.

What the law requires for everyone:

Under BEEG §1(1), a person is entitled to Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they meet all four of these conditions:
1. They have a residence or habitual abode in Germany ("einen Wohnsitz oder seinen gewöhnlichen Aufenthalt in Deutschland").
2. They live in one household with the child.
3. They care for and raise the child themselves.
4. They work not at all or not full-time ("keine oder keine volle Erwerbstätigkeit").

Under §1(6), a person is not working full-time if any of these applies:
- they work no more than 32 hours a week on average over the child's month of life;
- they are in employment for vocational training;
- they work as a suitable childminder within the meaning of §§23 and 43 SGB VIII.

Under §1(7), a foreign national without EU free-movement rights is entitled only if one of these applies:
1. They hold a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit.
2. They hold an EU Blue Card, an ICT card, a mobile ICT card, or a residence permit that entitles or entitled them to work for at least six months. This ground does not apply to permits issued for certain purposes listed in the statute: training, au pair or seasonal work, European voluntary service, job search, or recognition of foreign qualifications. It also does not apply to permits for study, and some recognition and job-search permits, where the person is not working, not on parental leave, and not receiving SGB III cash benefits. Permits issued under §23(1), §23a or §25(3) to (5) of the Residence Act are excluded too.
3. They hold one of those §23, §23a or §25 permits and are lawfully employed, on parental leave, or receiving SGB III cash benefits.
4. They hold one of those permits and have stayed in Germany lawfully, with permission, or with toleration for at least 15 months.
5. They hold an employment toleration under §60d with §60a(2) sentence 3 of the Residence Act.

Under §1(8), entitlement lapses if taxable income in the last completed assessment period before the birth was more than 175 000 euros. Where another person also meets the conditions, the combined taxable income of both people counts against that same limit ("mehr als 175 000 Euro").

Under §4(4), a parent is entitled to Elterngeld only if they claim it for at least two months of the child's life.

Under §7(1), Elterngeld must be applied for in writing. It is paid retroactively only for the last three months of life before the month in which the application is received ("rückwirkend nur für die letzten drei Lebensmonate"). Earlier months are not paid.

Who decides: the Elterngeldstelle for your district decides whether you are entitled. Approach that office about your application.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
This service cannot calculate how much tax you would save by switching to tax class III, or say whether you should switch. Tax class choice and any tax saved belong to a Steuerberater or your Finanzamt.

The excerpts do explain how a tax class change before the birth is treated when Elterngeld is calculated.

- The calculation uses your newest tax class ("kommt es auf die neueste Steuerklasse an").
- The older tax class is used only if it applied for longer within the whole assessment period ("Die ältere Steuerklasse wird nur dann verwendet, wenn diese innerhalb des gesamten Bemessungszeitraums länger gegolten hat als die neuere").
- For employment income, the assessment period is the twelve calendar months before the month of the birth ("die zwölf Kalendermonate vor dem Kalendermonat der Geburt des Kindes"). The statute sets out exceptions. Certain months are left out, for example periods of maternity protection or illness caused by the pregnancy. A different period applies if you also had self-employment income.
- Tax class VI is not taken into account ("die Steuerklasse VI bleibt unberücksichtigt").
- If you work after the birth, the same deduction details are used as before the birth. Changing tax class again after the birth no longer affects your Elterngeld.

What this means for your Elterngeld amount is decided by the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your district. For the tax effect of switching, ask a Steuerberater or your Finanzamt.
